2.title: LORE knowledge mode — exam convention (PYQ keys) (tier K)

K1.text: The **commonest site** of peptic ulcer perforation is the **anterior wall of the first part of the duodenum**.

K2.text: **Anterior** duodenal ulcers tend to **perforate**; **posterior** duodenal ulcers tend to **bleed** (erosion of the **gastroduodenal artery**).

K3.text: Perforated peptic ulcer is the **most common cause of pneumoperitoneum** (free intraperitoneal gas).

K4.text: Onset is **sudden, severe epigastric pain** that rapidly becomes generalised, with **board-like rigidity** and a patient who **lies still**.

K5.text: **Erect chest X-ray** is the first investigation and shows **free gas under the diaphragm** in roughly three-quarters of cases.

K6.text: **CT abdomen** is the most sensitive investigation for free gas and the **investigation of choice** when the X-ray is equivocal.

K7.text: Absence of free gas on X-ray does **not exclude** perforation.

K8.text: Standard operation is **closure with an omental patch** (Graham / Cellan-Jones repair) plus **peritoneal lavage**, open or laparoscopic.

K9.text: After repair, **H. pylori eradication** and a **PPI** prevent recurrence; routine definitive acid-reducing surgery is no longer needed.

K10.text: A peptic ulcer that erodes through the full thickness of the stomach or duodenal wall into the **free peritoneal cavity**.

K11.text: A perforation that is walled off by adjacent organs (omentum, liver, gallbladder) is a **sealed (contained) perforation**.

K12.text: **NSAIDs** (including low-dose aspirin) are a major cause, especially in the **elderly**.

K13.text: ***Helicobacter pylori*** infection is the other main cause of the underlying ulcer.

K14.text: **Smoking** is a risk factor for perforation.

K15.text: **Corticosteroids**, particularly combined with NSAIDs, add risk and can **mask the physical signs** of peritonitis.

K16.text: **Crack cocaine** use is associated with perforation in younger patients.

K17.text: Physiological stress (burns, head injury, critical illness) causes stress ulcers that may perforate; **Curling's ulcer** follows **burns** and **Cushing's ulcer** follows **head injury / raised intracranial pressure**.

K18.text: Gastroduodenal contents (acid, bile, enzymes) entering the peritoneum cause an initial **chemical peritonitis**.

K19.text: Bacterial contamination follows over hours, converting it to **bacterial (suppurative) peritonitis** and sepsis.

K20.text: Classic clinical course has three stages: **(1) prostration/chemical peritonitis**, **(2) reaction** (an apparent improvement as peritoneal exudate dilutes the irritant), **(3) diffuse bacterial peritonitis**.

K21.text: The "period of reaction" can mislead the clinician into thinking the patient is improving.

K22.text: Gastric contents may track down the **right paracolic gutter** to the right iliac fossa, mimicking **acute appendicitis** (**Valentino's syndrome**).

K23.text: Gas escaping through the perforation rises to lie beneath the diaphragm on standing, producing **pneumoperitoneum**.

K24.text: **Sudden-onset, severe epigastric pain**, often with a precise remembered time of onset, spreading over the whole abdomen.

K25.text: There may be a preceding history of dyspepsia or NSAID use, though many patients have **no prior ulcer history**.

K26.text: **Shoulder-tip pain** from diaphragmatic irritation (referred via the **phrenic nerve, C3–C5**).

K27.text: The patient **lies still** because movement worsens peritoneal pain (contrast with the restless patient of colic).

K28.text: **Board-like (generalised) rigidity** with marked guarding and tenderness.

K29.text: **Obliteration (loss) of liver dullness** on percussion from free gas.

K30.text: **Absent or reduced bowel sounds** as ileus develops.

K31.text: Tachycardia, hypotension and fever appear as bacterial peritonitis and sepsis develop.

K32.text: Signs may be **blunted in the elderly, immunosuppressed or those on steroids**.

K33.text: **Erect chest X-ray**: free gas under the diaphragm (**pneumoperitoneum**), best seen under the **right hemidiaphragm**.

K34.text: The patient should sit upright for about **10 minutes** before the erect film to let gas rise.

K35.text: An erect chest X-ray can detect as little as about **1–2 mL** of free gas.

K36.text: If the patient cannot sit up, a **left lateral decubitus** abdominal film shows gas between the liver and the lateral abdominal wall.

K37.text: Signs of pneumoperitoneum on a supine film include **Rigler's sign** (both sides of the bowel wall visible), the **football sign** and the **falciform ligament sign**.

K38.text: **Chilaiditi sign** (colon interposed between liver and diaphragm) is a **pseudo-pneumoperitoneum** and must not be mistaken for free gas.

K39.text: **CT abdomen** is the most sensitive test, detects small volumes of free gas and fluid, and often localises the site.

K40.text: A **water-soluble contrast (Gastrografin) study** can show whether a perforation has sealed, when conservative management is considered.

K41.text: **Serum amylase** may be mildly raised in perforation, so it should be measured to help separate it from acute pancreatitis (where it is usually markedly raised).

K42.text: Baseline bloods (FBC, urea/electrolytes, lactate, group and save, blood gas) guide resuscitation.

K43.text: Barium is **contraindicated** when perforation is suspected because barium peritonitis is severe.

K44.text: **Resuscitation first**: IV access and crystalloid fluids, **nasogastric tube** aspiration, urinary catheter for output monitoring, analgesia.

K45.text: **IV broad-spectrum antibiotics** and an **IV proton pump inhibitor** are started on diagnosis.

K46.text: **Surgery is the standard treatment** for free perforation with peritonitis.

K47.text: The perforation is closed with an **omental patch**: the **Graham patch** uses a free omental plug and the **Cellan-Jones repair** uses a **pedicled tongue of omentum** sutured over the defect.

K48.text: In exam usage the pedicled omental patch closure is commonly called **"Graham's patch"**.

K49.text: **Thorough peritoneal lavage** with warm saline is done at the end of repair.

K50.text: **Laparoscopic repair** is an accepted alternative to open repair in suitable, stable patients.

K51.text: A **gastric ulcer perforation** should be **biopsied or excised** because it may be a **perforated gastric carcinoma**.

K52.text: **Conservative (non-operative) management** — nasogastric suction, IV fluids, antibiotics, PPI (the **Taylor method**) — is reserved for selected stable patients with a **sealed perforation** confirmed on contrast study.

K53.text: Conservative management is unsuitable for the elderly and for those not improving within about 12–24 hours, who need surgery.

K54.text: Postoperatively, test for and **eradicate *H. pylori***, stop NSAIDs where possible and continue a PPI.

K55.text: **Definitive acid-reducing surgery** (vagotomy) at the time of perforation is **no longer routine** in the PPI and *H. pylori* era.

K56.text: Large ("giant") perforations, commonly described as larger than about 2 cm, may not be closable by a patch and may need **partial gastrectomy** or other techniques.

K57.text: **Boey score** predicts mortality using three factors: **shock on admission** (systolic BP <100 mmHg), **major co-existing medical illness**, and **delay to surgery over 24 hours**.

K58.text: Mortality rises with **age, delay to surgery, shock and comorbidity**.

K63.text: Recurrent ulceration if *H. pylori* is not eradicated or NSAIDs continue.

K78.text: PYQs have expected "Graham's patch" as the operation for perforated duodenal ulcer; strictly, Graham described a **free omental graft** and the **pedicled** omental patch is the **Cellan-Jones** repair, but either name scores as "omental patch closure".

K79.text: PYQs have expected **erect chest X-ray** as the first / initial investigation and sometimes as the "investigation of choice"; current practice treats **CT abdomen** as the most sensitive investigation and the test of choice when doubt remains.

K80.text: PYQs often quote free gas under the diaphragm in about **70%** of perforations; texts vary, so treat the figure as approximate and remember a normal film does **not exclude** perforation.

K81.text: PYQs have offered **vagotomy with drainage** or **partial gastrectomy** as options; current practice is simple omental patch closure with *H. pylori* eradication and PPI, not definitive acid-reducing surgery.

K82.text: Shoulder-tip pain here is from diaphragmatic irritation; **Kehr's sign** (left shoulder pain) is the eponym tied to **splenic rupture**, a common distractor.

K83.text: A **perforated gastric ulcer** must be biopsied because the exam's trap answer is to treat it like a duodenal ulcer and miss **carcinoma**.
